1: # Instructions
2: 
3: Reparent a tree on a selected node.
4: 
5: A [tree][wiki-tree] is a special type of [graph][wiki-graph] where all nodes are connected but there are no cycles.
6: That means, there is exactly one path to get from one node to another for any pair of nodes.
7: 
8: This exercise is all about re-orientating a tree to see things from a different point of view.
9: For example family trees are usually presented from the ancestor's perspective:
10: 
11: ```text
12:     +------0------+
13:     |      |      |
14:   +-1-+  +-2-+  +-3-+
15:   |   |  |   |  |   |
16:   4   5  6   7  8   9
17: ```
18: 
19: But there is no inherent direction in a tree.
20: The same information can be presented from the perspective of any other node in the tree, by pulling it up to the root and dragging its relationships along with it.
21: So the same tree from 6's perspective would look like:
22: 
23: ```text
24:         6
25:         |
26:   +-----2-----+
27:   |           |
28:   7     +-----0-----+
29:         |           |
30:       +-1-+       +-3-+
31:       |   |       |   |
32:       4   5       8   9
33: ```
34: 
35: This lets us more simply describe the paths between two nodes.
36: So for example the path from 6-9 (which in the first tree goes up to the root and then down to a different leaf node) can be seen to follow the path 6-2-0-3-9.
37: 
38: This exercise involves taking an input tree and re-orientating it from the point of view of one of the nodes.
39: 
40: [wiki-graph]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_(graph_theory)
41: [wiki-tree]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_(discrete_mathematics)

     def __eq__(self, other):
         return self.__dict__() == other.__dict__()
 
+    def _contains(self, label):
+        return self.label == label or any(
+            child._contains(label) for child in self.children
+        )
+

-        pass

Done. All 15 tests in `pov_test.py` pass, and I only modified `pov.py` (no new files, tests untouched).

## What I implemented

**`from_pov(from_node)`** — reorients the tree so `from_node` becomes the root:
- `_find_path` locates the path from the current root down to the target (a list of nodes), returning `None` if the target doesn't exist → raises `ValueError("Tree could not be reoriented")`.
- It then rebuilds bottom-up from the original root toward the target. Each node keeps its original children except the one on the path, and gains the accumulated subtree as its last child — so the target ends up on top with the whole ancestor chain dragged beneath it.

**`path_to(from_node, to_node)`** — reorients via `from_pov(from_node)`, then walks down from the new root to `to_node`, collecting labels. If the destination isn't present it raises `ValueError("No path found")`; a missing source is caught earlier by `from_pov` with the "Tree could not be reoriented" message, matching the tests.

Two helpers support this: `_contains` (does this subtree hold a label?) and `_path_to` (returns the label path from a node to a descendant).

The existing `__eq__`/`__dict__` already compare trees with children sorted, so child ordering doesn't affect equality — which is why the rebuild order is flexible.

One note: my first recursive attempt appended every ancestor directly under the new root instead of nesting them along the path, so I switched to the path-rebuild approach, which handles the deeply-nested and cousin cases correctly.
